nameStory: The flat-clawed hermit crab gets its name from its most distinctive feature - unusually broad, flattened claws that look like they've been pressed in a vise! These wide, flat claws are perfectly shaped to fit together like puzzle pieces, creating a living door that seals the crab safely inside its borrowed shell home. You might also hear it called the 'shield hermit crab' because those flat claws work just like a protective shield.
description: The flat-clawed hermit crab is a pale, off-white crustacean that makes its home in empty snail shells along New England's coast. Like all hermit crabs, it has a soft, vulnerable abdomen that it protects by backing into discarded shells - particularly those of shark eye snails and whelks. This species grows to about 1.2 inches long, making it one of the larger hermit crabs you'll encounter in tidal pools. Its most striking feature is its pair of dramatically flattened claws that look nothing like the typical pincer claws of other crabs.

idTips.label: Flat, broad claws
idTips.description: The claws are remarkably wide and flattened, almost like tiny shields, and can lock together perfectly to seal the shell opening when the crab retreats inside

idTips.label: Unequal claw sizes
idTips.description: One claw is noticeably larger than the other, though both have that characteristic flattened shape that feels smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Pale coloration
idTips.description: The body appears off-white to very pale gray, sometimes with a slightly translucent quality that makes it blend with sandy shell interiors

idTips.label: Shell preference
idTips.description: Almost always found in the smooth, round shells of shark eye snails or the spiral shells of whelks, which feel heavy and substantial in your hand

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Reaches up to 1.2 inches in length, making it feel more substantial than the tiny hermit crabs often found higher in the intertidal zone

habitat: Look for flat-clawed hermit crabs in the lower intertidal zone and shallow subtidal areas along New England's rocky and sandy coastlines. They prefer areas with good shell availability, often near beds of whelks and moon snails whose empty shells they depend on for homes. You'll most commonly spot them during low tide in tide pools, under rocks, or scuttling across sandy bottoms in shallow water.

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures warm, often seen moving between shells as they outgrow their current homes during this growth period.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're easily found in tide pools and shallow water, actively foraging and most responsive to gentle handling.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper water, though still findable in protected tide pools during warm autumn days.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and typically in deeper water, rarely encountered in the intertidal zone during cold months.

funFact: Flat-clawed hermit crabs often share their shell homes with zebra flatworms - colorful striped hitchhikers that live harmlessly alongside the crab, creating a tiny underwater apartment complex in a single shell!
confusionNotes: The flat, shield-like claws immediately distinguish this species from the long-claw hermit crab, which has thin, elongated pincers, and the Acadian hermit crab, which has more typical rounded claws. Remember: if the claws look like they could be used as tiny spatulas, you've found a flat-clawed hermit!
contextualKnowledge: Despite having many common names (gray, shield, thumb-clawed, broad-clawed, and warty hermit crab), 'flat-clawed' is the most descriptive and widely used name that directly points to its key identifying feature.
compareHints: Among New England's hermit crabs, the flat-clawed hermit is unmistakable due to its shield-like claws - the long-claw hermit has thin, extended claws, while the Acadian hermit has more typical rounded pincers. The flat-clawed is also generally larger and paler than its relatives, and shows a strong preference for the substantial shells of moon snails and whelks rather than the smaller periwinkle and cerith shells favored by other species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's hermit crabs, the Long-claw is distinguished by its notably slender, elongated claws compared to the Flat-clawed Hermit Crab's broad, flattened pincers.
Compared to its close relative the Long-claw Hermit Crab, the Acadian hermit has a more robust build and prefers colder waters further north.
Among New England's hermit crabs, the hairy hermit is the only one with distinctly fuzzy, bristled legs - its relatives like the Long-claw and Flat-clawed hermit crabs have smooth legs and claws.

Unlike its relatives the Long-claw Hermit (which has elongated claws) and Flat-clawed Hermit (which has flattened, broad claws), the Brown Banded Hermit has proportionally normal-sized claws but sports those unmistakable brown leg bands.
